בתת.
גאר
have been derived from the nature of
the place.
* בָּתַת obsol. root, Arab. بَتَّ I, IV, to
cut, to cut off, to break off, comp. under
r. בָּדַד I; بَتَاتٌ something broken off,
finished, destroyed, بَتَّةً and الْبَتَّةَ whol-
ly, entirely. In Hebrew it seems to
have signified:
1. to cut or mark out, to define, and
hence to measure; whence בַּת II, as a
measure of liquids.
2. to cut off any thing, to make an end
of, to lay wholly waste, i. q. כִּלָּה; whence
בָּתָה, בַּתָּה.
ג
Gimel, גִּימֶל, the third letter of the
Hebrew alphabet; as a numeral denot-
ing 3. Its name differs only in form
from גָּמָל camel; and its figure in Pheni-
cian inscriptions (Λ, Λ,) bears a cer-
tain resemblance to the camel’s hump
or neck; see Monumen. Phœn. p. 22.
As the softest of the palatal letters
(גיכק) except Yod, it is often inter-
changed: a) With the harder palatals
כ and ק, both in the Hebrew itself,
and in the corresponding forms of the
kindred dialects; e. g. גָּדִישׁ, جُدْس,
كَدِيس, a heap of sheaves; גָּפְרִית,
ܟܶܒܪܺܝܬܳܐ, كِبْرِيت, sulphur; גָּנַן and כָּנַן
to cover, to protect; גָּנַז and כָּנַס, كنز,
to collect, to heap up: רָגַל and רָכַל to run
up and down, גָּבִיעַ, قُبْعَة, calix of flow-
ers; גָּדַד, جَلَّ and قَلَّ to cut; שָׁקֵד,
שִׁגֵּד, ܫܶܓܕܳܐ, an almond-tree.
b) More rarely with the gutturals; as
ע, e. g. נָבַע, Chald. נְבַע, נְבַג, to burst
forth; גָּרָה, Arab. غَرِىَ to provoke; also ח,
e. g. אֶפְרֹחַ, ܦܰܪܽܘܓܳܐ, young of birds;
comp. אֶחָח.
גֵּא m. adj. for גֵּאֶה (r. גָּאָה) elated, i. e.
haughty, proud, Is. 16, 6.
* גָּאָה fut. יִגְאֶה, a poetic word.
1. to lift up oneself, to rise, to increase,
e. g. of rising waters Ez. 47, 5; of a
plant growing Job 8, 11.—Job 10, 16
וְיִגְאֶה כַּשַּׁחַל תְּצוּדֵנִי and if it lift up itself
(sc. my head) thou huntest me as a lion.
2. Metaph. to be exalted, majestic,
glorious, spoken of God, Ex. 15, 1. 21.—
Hence in the derivatives also:
3. to be eminent, excellent, splendid;
see deriv. גָּאוֹן no. 2.
4. to be elated, i. e. haughty, proud;
see deriv. גֵּאֶה no. 2, גַּאֲוָה and גָּאוֹן no. 3.
Syr. Pa. ܓܰܐܺܝ to decorate, to make
splendid, magnificent; Ethpa. to boast
oneself; ܓܰܐ̣ܐ, ܓܰܐܝܳܐ decorated, elegant,
magnificent. In the signif. of pride it
corresponds with Gr. γαίω.
Deriv. גֵּא, גֵּוָה I, and those here fol-
lowing.
גֵּאֶה adj. 1. lifted up, high, lofty,
וְהַשְׁפִּילֵהוּ look upon every high thing
and bring it low.
2. elated, i. e. proud, haughty, Jer. 48,
29. Plur. גֵּאִים the proud, often with the
accessory notion of impiety, ungodli-
ness; as elsewhere gentleness and hu-
mility include also the idea of piety, see
19. Sept. ὑπερήφανοι, ὑβρισταί.
גֵּאָה f. pride, haughtiness, Prov. 8, 13.
גְּאוּאֵל (majesty of God) Geuel pr. n.
גַּאֲוָה f. (r. גָּאָה) pr. elevation, exalta-
tion; hence
1. majesty, glory, as of God, Deut. 33
2. ornament, excellency, splendour,
3. pride, haughtiness; Ps. 73, 6 לָכֵן
עֲנָקַתְמוֹ גַאֲוָה therefore pride surroundeth
them like a neck-chain; i. e. clothes their
neck, as being the seat of pride. Ps. 31,

line_status.note: The kaf carries a single dot (hiriq) beneath it, not a qamets, and the lamed has a dagesh with qamets — the Piel form כִּלָּה, matching Reading A.

The mark after גָּפְרִית is a comma with a descending tail, not a period; the list continues onto the next line with كِبْرِيت, sulphur. Everything else (Arabic كَدِيس with its points, the Hebrew vowels, dagesh in gimel, plene yod) is identical in both readings and matches the print.
The line begins with a pointed Syriac word (visible at far left, with vowel points printed) which Reading B omits; and the Hebrew pair is גָּנַן / כָּנַן — the middle letter is a narrow nun, not bet.
Over the Arabic bāʾ the print shows a small circle (sukūn), not a fatḥa; the fatḥa sits over the ʿayn. So قُبْعَة (Reading B), not قُبَعَة.
Shin has a single dot beneath (hiriq, not tsere) and the gimel carries a dagesh with tsere; Syriac ܫܶܓܕܳܐ is printed with points as both readings give.

Under the nun of the third Hebrew word (נְבַג) the print shows two vertical dots (shewa), matching the preceding Chaldee נְבַע — not a qamets as Reading A has. Both are Chaldee forms, so the shewa is expected; the first word נָבַע does carry a qamets.

The Hebrew is גָּרָה with a resh (rounded shoulder, no dagesh in the second letter), not גִּדָּה; the Arabic final letter is printed dotless (ى) with fatha, and the last Hebrew letter is ח (closed top-left corner), not ה. There is a space before the semicolon in "provoke ;".

Syriac 4th letter is gamal ܓ (long down-left tail), not ܚܬ — A's word is right; but the print has a space before the final semicolon ("birds ;") as in B. Hebrew אֶפְרֹחַ identical in both and matches the print.

The vowel under the middle ח is a qamets (horizontal bar with a short descending stem, T-shaped), not a patach (plain horizontal bar); segol under א is printed as both readings have it, and no other points or dagesh are present.

The first Syriac word is printed with two plain vertical strokes (alaph alaph) after gamal — three letters, no yod — and the second word has gamal, alaph, a short yod, alaph (four letters). Reading A reverses the order and gives the second word a final yod; Reading B's letter skeletons and order match the print. Vowel marks (point above gamal, dot below first word, marks on second word) are consistent with B.
The final mark after "31" has a curved tail descending below the baseline (compare the round dots after "pride" and "Ps"), so it is a comma, not a full stop — Reading B is correct.
